metadata.title: Orthopaedic Mini-OSCE Past Questions Q-Bank
metadata.description: Multiple-choice questions organized by topics and chapters.

questions.question: The special test used to diagnose this condition is called :
questions.explanation: The image shows the Achilles tendon and its insertion on the calcaneus. Rupture of the Achilles tendon is confirmed by the Thompson (Simmonds) calf-squeeze test: squeezing the calf of a prone patient normally causes plantar flexion; absence of movement indicates a complete tendon rupture. The slide's handwritten note beside the answer reads 'Achilles tendon'.

optionExplanations.A: Thomas test detects a fixed flexion deformity of the hip; it does not test the Achilles tendon.
optionExplanations.B: Trendelenburg test assesses hip abductor (gluteus medius/minimus) function.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The Thompson calf-squeeze test is the clinical test for Achilles tendon rupture.
optionExplanations.D: Finkelstein test is used for De Quervain tenosynovitis of the wrist.
optionExplanations.E: Kocher is a name attached to the criteria for septic hip in children and to a shoulder reduction manoeuvre; it is not an Achilles test.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise Achilles tendon rupture and name the Thompson test as its diagnostic clinical test.

questions.question: In this case , All of the following are True EXCEPT:

options.A: CT scan is advised to get a clear picture of the situation of the wrist joint.
options.B: If not treated well by anatomical reduction and fixation it could end of osteoarthritis
options.C: We can see a step and a separation in articular surface
options.D: Operation within six hours is an emergency

questions.explanation: The radiograph shows a wrist with a step and separation of the articular surface, i.e. an intra-articular wrist injury. Such injuries need CT for articular detail, anatomical reduction and fixation, and if poorly reduced lead to post-traumatic osteoarthritis. They are urgent but not a six-hour emergency (unlike open fractures, vascular compromise or compartment syndrome), so surgery is usually done within days once swelling allows. (The slide does not name the exact injury.)

optionExplanations.A: True. CT gives a clearer picture of articular congruity and fragments in an intra-articular wrist injury.
optionExplanations.B: True. Residual articular incongruity predisposes to post-traumatic osteoarthritis.
optionExplanations.C: True. A step-off and gap in the articular surface are visible on the image and are the reason anatomical reduction is required.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Surgery within six hours is not required for a closed intra-articular wrist injury without vascular or neurological compromise.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand the principles of managing intra-articular wrist injuries (CT, anatomical reduction, timing of surgery).

questions.question: The best management of this 14 years old boy, with knee pain without trauma, no fever, is:
questions.explanation: A 14-year-old with activity-related anterior knee pain, no trauma and no fever, and a lateral radiograph with the arrow at the tibial tuberosity, fits Osgood-Schlatter disease (traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity). It is self-limiting; the treatment is activity modification and rest, analgesia and stretching/strengthening.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Rest and reduced physical activity is the standard first-line management; the condition resolves with skeletal maturity.
optionExplanations.B: Cortisone infiltration is not recommended; it risks tendon weakening and is unnecessary.
optionExplanations.C: Casting is rarely needed and only for severe cases; it is not the best management.
optionExplanations.D: MRI and surgery are unnecessary; surgery is reserved for rare persistent symptomatic ossicles after skeletal maturity.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage Osgood-Schlatter disease conservatively with activity modification.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: Such condition may appear in which age group?
questions.explanation: The radiograph (red circle over the greater tuberosity region) shows calcific deposition in the rotator cuff, i.e. calcific tendinitis. It typically affects adults in the 40-50 year range (range about 30-60 years) and is more common in women.

optionExplanations.A: 0-10 years is not an age of presentation for calcific tendinitis.
optionExplanations.B: 10-20 years is unusual for this condition.
optionExplanations.C: 20-30 years is uncommon; incidence rises after 30 years.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Peak incidence is 40-50 years.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall the typical age group of calcific tendinitis of the shoulder.

questions.question: All are special tests to diagnose this condition EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The image (hand with numbness over the median nerve distribution and pain) represents carpal tunnel syndrome. Carpal tunnel compression test (Durkan), Phalen's and Tinel's tests are provocative tests for median nerve compression at the wrist. Allen's test assesses the patency of the radial and ulnar arteries, not nerve compression.

optionExplanations.A: A valid test: the carpal compression (nerve compression) test reproduces symptoms in carpal tunnel syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: A valid test: Phalen's (wrist flexion) test reproduces median nerve symptoms.
optionExplanations.C: A valid test: Tinel's sign (tapping over the median nerve) reproduces paraesthesia.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Allen's test evaluates arterial supply to the hand, not carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the clinical provocative tests for carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.question: All are special tests to diagnose this condition EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The image shows median nerve territory numbness and pain (carpal tunnel syndrome). Nerve compression, Phalen's and Tinel's tests are used to diagnose it. The Hawkins-Kennedy test is a shoulder impingement test.

optionExplanations.A: A valid test for carpal tunnel syndrome (carpal compression test).
optionExplanations.B: A valid test (Phalen's).
optionExplanations.C: A valid test (Tinel's).
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Hawkins-Kennedy is a test for subacromial impingement of the shoulder.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate wrist nerve-compression tests from shoulder impingement tests.

questions.question: All are true about this condition EXCEPT :
questions.explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome may follow wrist trauma, is associated with diabetes, and is usually confirmed with nerve conduction studies. Initial treatment is conservative (night splinting, steroid injection); surgical release is indicated after failed conservative treatment, constant numbness, or thenar wasting, not immediately in every case.

optionExplanations.A: True. Previous wrist trauma (e.g. distal radius fracture) can cause carpal tunnel syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: True. Diabetes is a recognised association.
optionExplanations.C: True per the source: nerve conduction studies are used to confirm and grade the condition.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Immediate surgery is not the standard approach; conservative treatment comes first unless there are severe or progressive deficits.

questions.educationalObjective: Outline the associations and staged management of carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: Regarding tetanus prophylaxis in a 26 years old male patient suffering from an open femur fracture with very dirty wound 11 cm long. • He has unknown history of previous vaccination Tetanus prophylaxis for this patient should consist of:

options.D: No prophylaxis is required in this patient

questions.explanation: An open femoral fracture with a very dirty 11 cm wound is a tetanus-prone wound. With an unknown vaccination history the patient should receive both passive immunisation (tetanus immunoglobulin) and active immunisation (tetanus toxoid vaccine), in addition to antibiotics and debridement.

optionExplanations.A: Active immunisation alone is enough only for clean minor wounds or for patients with a complete primary course.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Unknown immunisation status plus a tetanus-prone (dirty) wound needs tetanus immunoglobulin and the vaccine.
optionExplanations.C: Passive immunisation alone gives temporary protection but does not start active immunity.
optionExplanations.D: Prophylaxis is always required in a dirty open fracture.

questions.educationalObjective: Select tetanus prophylaxis for a tetanus-prone wound with unknown vaccination history.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: Regarding this 15 years old male patient suffering from isolated open femur fracture with dirty wound 11 cm long. Best management option:

options.B: IV antibiotics, debridement, tetanus vaccine then internal fixation
options.C: IV antibiotics, tetanus vaccine and internal fixation, and wound management
options.D: IV antibiotics, tetanus vaccine, debridement , external fixation, and wound management

questions.explanation: A grossly contaminated 11 cm open femoral fracture is a high-grade (Gustilo III) injury. Management includes IV antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, formal surgical debridement, skeletal stabilisation with external fixation (temporary or definitive depending on the wound) and wound management (delayed closure/coverage). Primary internal fixation of a dirty wound without debridement risks deep infection.

optionExplanations.A: Omits debridement, tetanus prophylaxis and wound care; internal fixation of a dirty wound is unsafe.
optionExplanations.B: Includes debridement but proceeds directly to internal fixation of a contaminated wound and omits wound management.
optionExplanations.C: Omits debridement; internal fixation without it risks infection.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Antibiotics, tetanus vaccine, debridement, external fixation and wound management is the complete approach.

questions.educationalObjective: Describe the initial management of a contaminated open long-bone fracture.

questions.question: This 25 yr old football player is unable to extend his Lt knee after rotational injury, One of the following is not a positive diagnostic criterion for this injury:
questions.explanation: Inability to extend the knee after a rotational injury indicates a locked knee, typically from a displaced meniscal (bucket-handle) tear. Meniscal injury is supported by a positive Apley grinding test, medial joint-line tenderness and MRI. Lachman's test assesses the anterior cruciate ligament and is not a diagnostic criterion for a meniscal tear.

optionExplanations.A: A positive Apley's grinding test supports a meniscal tear.
optionExplanations.B: MRI is the imaging test that confirms a meniscal tear.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Lachman's test is an ACL test, not a criterion for a meniscal tear.
optionExplanations.D: Medial joint-line tenderness supports a medial meniscal tear.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify diagnostic criteria for a meniscal tear versus ligament tests.

questions.question: All of the following are complications of the condition shown in the pic EXCEPT?
questions.explanation: The MRI shows bilateral distal tibial/ankle pathology; the source does not name the condition. The listed complications (physeal arrest, septic arthritis, pathological fracture) are typical of metaphyseal bone infection/lesions in children. A stress fracture is a fatigue injury from repetitive loading and is not a complication of such a condition. [FLAG - Uncertain / ambiguous: The slide does not name the condition shown on the MRI; the explanation assumes physeal/metaphyseal bone infection. The source key (C) was kept.]

optionExplanations.A: Physeal arrest (growth disturbance) is a recognised complication of metaphyseal pathology near the physis.
optionExplanations.B: Septic arthritis can follow spread from adjacent metaphyseal infection.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Stress fracture arises from repetitive loading of normal bone, not as a complication of this condition.
optionExplanations.D: A weakened bone may fracture pathologically.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise complications of metaphyseal bone pathology in children.

questions.question: All of the following are treatment options of this condition except:
questions.explanation: The radiograph (arrow on the plantar calcaneus) shows a calcaneal spur at the plantar fascia origin, i.e. plantar fasciitis. Treatment is conservative: weight reduction, stretching physiotherapy, heel cushions/supportive footwear, and steroid infiltration for refractory cases. Flat (unsupportive) shoes aggravate symptoms and are not a treatment.

optionExplanations.A: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Flat, hard-soled shoes are not a treatment; cushioned heel supports or supportive shoes are advised.
optionExplanations.B: Weight reduction lowers load on the plantar fascia and is recommended.
optionExplanations.C: Physiotherapy with plantar fascia and calf stretching is first-line.
optionExplanations.D: Local steroid infiltration may be used in resistant cases.

questions.educationalObjective: List the non-operative treatment options for plantar fasciitis/heel spur.

questions.question: All of the following are True for this patient EXCEPT:

options.D: cortisone injections can help relieve symptoms

questions.explanation: Plantar fasciitis with a heel spur causes heel pain that is worst with the first steps in the morning or after rest, usually easing with walking. It often resolves with stretching, and cortisone injections can relieve symptoms. Pain that is worse with activity is not the typical pattern.

optionExplanations.A: True. Pain is classically worst in the morning on first steps.
optionExplanations.B: True. Calf and plantar fascia stretching exercises often lead to resolution.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Pain typically improves with activity once the fascia 'warms up' rather than worsening.
optionExplanations.D: True. Corticosteroid injection can give symptomatic relief.

questions.educationalObjective: Describe the typical symptom pattern of plantar fasciitis.

questions.question: One of the treatment options is FALSE
questions.explanation: For painful heel spur/plantar fasciitis, injections, shock wave therapy and (for refractory cases) surgical excision/release are used. Subtalar arthrodesis (fusion) is not a treatment for this condition.

optionExplanations.A: A valid treatment option (steroid infiltration).
optionExplanations.B: A valid option for resistant cases (excision of the spur/fascia release).
optionExplanations.C: A valid treatment option (extracorporeal shock wave therapy).
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the FALSE option). Subtalar fusion is used for hindfoot arthritis or deformity, not heel spurs.

questions.educationalObjective: Know which treatments are appropriate for heel spur pain.

questions.question: The test shown on both illustration photos is known as:
questions.explanation: The photographs show the Thomas test: with the patient supine, the opposite hip is fully flexed to flatten the lumbar lordosis; failure of the tested thigh to lie flat reveals a fixed flexion deformity of the hip.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The sequence shows the Thomas test for hip flexion contracture.
optionExplanations.B: 'Thombson' appears to be a misspelling of Thompson, the Achilles calf-squeeze test.
optionExplanations.C: Trendelenburg test assesses hip abductors in single-leg stance.
optionExplanations.D: FABER (Patrick) test assesses hip/sacroiliac pathology with the leg figure-of-four.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise the Thomas test.

questions.question: The test shown will be positive in patients with:
questions.explanation: The Thomas test unmasks a fixed flexion deformity of the hip, as seen in hip arthritis (including with anterior osteophytes) or hip flexor contracture. It is not a test for knee arthritis, iliotibial band tightness (Ober's test) or DDH in children (Ortolani/Barlow).

optionExplanations.A: Knee arthritis is not assessed by the Thomas test.
optionExplanations.B: Iliotibial band contracture is tested with Ober's test.
optionExplanations.C: DDH in children is assessed with Ortolani/Barlow and Galeazzi signs.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Hip arthritis with anterior osteophytes causes fixed flexion that the Thomas test reveals.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the indication for the Thomas test.

questions.question: Best therapy option of this condition is:
questions.explanation: The hand shows fixed flexion of the ring finger consistent with Dupuytren's contracture. Definitive treatment of a symptomatic flexion contracture is surgical (fasciectomy/excision of diseased palmar fascia); collagenase injection or needle aponeurotomy are alternatives in selected patients.

optionExplanations.A: Correct per source. Surgical excision (fasciectomy) is the definitive therapy for a contracture.
optionExplanations.B: Steroid infiltration does not reverse a fixed contracture (steroids help trigger finger).
optionExplanations.C: Mobilisation under anaesthesia is used for frozen shoulder, not Dupuytren's.
optionExplanations.D: NSAIDs do not treat the fibromatosis.

questions.educationalObjective: State the treatment of established Dupuytren's contracture.

questions.question: This condition is usually:

options.D: associated with poor blood sugar control

questions.explanation: Dupuytren's contracture is associated with diabetes mellitus (poor glycaemic control), alcohol, smoking and epilepsy. It is not linked to obesity or rheumatoid arthritis, and release of the A1 pulley treats trigger finger rather than Dupuytren's disease.

optionExplanations.A: Obesity is not an established association.
optionExplanations.B: Rheumatoid arthritis is not an association of Dupuytren's disease.
optionExplanations.C: A1 pulley release treats trigger finger; Dupuytren's needs fascial excision.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Association with diabetes/poor blood sugar control is recognised.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall the risk associations of Dupuytren's contracture.

questions.question: ONE is TRUE:

options.A: cortisone injection is first line therapy
options.C: black people affected more than white people

questions.explanation: Dupuytren's disease is associated with uncontrolled diabetes. Corticosteroid injection is not first-line therapy, and the condition is more common in people of Northern European descent than in black people.

optionExplanations.A: Cortisone injection is not first-line therapy for Dupuytren's contracture.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Uncontrolled diabetes is a recognised risk factor.
optionExplanations.C: The condition is more common in white (Northern European) populations.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall epidemiology and risk factors for Dupuytren's contracture.

questions.question: One of these hip conditions does not cause this sign:
questions.explanation: The drawing shows a positive Trendelenburg sign (pelvic tilt in single-leg stance). It is caused by failure of the hip abductor mechanism: DDH, missed hip dislocation, superior gluteal nerve injury, abductor muscle tear. Shortening of the contralateral femur does not produce the sign. The answer was marked by yellow highlighting on the slide.

optionExplanations.A: DDH causes a positive Trendelenburg sign through loss of the abductor fulcrum.
optionExplanations.B: A missed hip dislocation disrupts the abductor mechanism and causes the sign.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the 'does not cause' answer). Contralateral femoral shortening does not impair the abductors.
optionExplanations.D: Superior gluteal nerve injury paralyses gluteus medius/minimus and causes the sign.
optionExplanations.E: A tear/injury of the abductor muscles causes the sign.

questions.educationalObjective: List causes of a positive Trendelenburg sign.

questions.question: One is TRUE:
questions.explanation: The illustration shows a Trendelenburg-type pelvic tilt in standing (viewed from behind); the pathology lies in the stance hip, as the abductors cannot hold the pelvis level. The source (yellow highlight) marks the left hip. The sign relates to the hip, not the sacroiliac joint. [FLAG - Uncertain / ambiguous: Laterality depends on the orientation of the illustration, which could only be checked against the source key (yellow highlight on option B).]

optionExplanations.A: Per the source the right hip is not the affected side in this drawing.
optionExplanations.B: Correct per source (yellow highlight). Pathology of the left hip.
optionExplanations.C: The sacroiliac joint is not the cause of a Trendelenburg sign.
optionExplanations.D: The sacroiliac joint is not the cause of a Trendelenburg sign.

questions.educationalObjective: Interpret a Trendelenburg sign and localise the affected hip.

questions.question: One of these hip conditions does not cause this sign:
questions.explanation: A positive Trendelenburg sign results from abductor failure: DDH, superior gluteal nerve injury, abductor dysfunction and Perthes disease (coxa breva with abductor insufficiency). The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus (hip extension) and does not cause the sign.

optionExplanations.A: DDH causes the sign.
optionExplanations.B: Superior gluteal nerve injury denervates gluteus medius/minimus and causes the sign.
optionExplanations.C: Abductor dysfunction is the direct mechanism.
optionExplanations.D: Perthes disease can cause an abductor lurch/positive sign.
optionExplanations.E: Correct (the 'does not cause' answer). The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, so injury causes weak extension, not a Trendelenburg sign.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate superior and inferior gluteal nerve injuries.

questions.question: This patient has this injury for 5 years, the best next management for such conditions is:

options.A: continue as treated before with oral antibiotcs

questions.explanation: A chronic foot wound present for five years in which oral antibiotics have failed suggests chronic osteomyelitis/chronic infection of bone. The best next step is surgical debridement of infected and necrotic tissue and bone, with cultures and targeted antibiotics. Amputation is reserved for failed debridement or unsalvageable limbs. [FLAG - Source formatting note: The source lists the options as A, B, C and E (no D); 'E. Amputation' was relabelled D.]

optionExplanations.A: Continuing oral antibiotics has already failed after five years.
optionExplanations.B: IV antibiotics alone cannot sterilise necrotic/devitalised bone.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Surgical debridement is the definitive next step.
optionExplanations.D: Amputation is a last resort when the limb is unsalvageable.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan surgical management of chronic osteomyelitis.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: 60 years old male patient, complaining from increased shoulder pain after prolonged immobilization, the diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Shoulder pain and stiffness after prolonged immobilisation in a 60-year-old is typical of adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder).

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Adhesive capsulitis commonly follows immobilisation and causes pain and global stiffness.
optionExplanations.B: Septic arthritis presents with fever, acute swelling and systemic illness.
optionExplanations.C: Calcific tendinitis causes acute severe pain with calcific deposits on X-ray.
optionExplanations.D: Impingement causes a painful arc rather than global stiffness after immobilisation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise adhesive capsulitis.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: Regarding these metals all of the following are true except:

options.A: Allows accurate reduction and maintenance of position
options.B: Allows the patient`s joints more mobility, avoiding joint stiffness

questions.explanation: The picture shows intramedullary nails/rods and a locking plate. Internal fixation gives accurate reduction and stable maintenance of position, allows early joint mobilisation, may encourage union and shortens hospital stay. These implants are not best used in paediatric patients, where growth plates make non-operative care or flexible/limited fixation preferred.

optionExplanations.A: True. Internal fixation gives accurate reduction and holds position.
optionExplanations.B: True. Stable fixation allows early joint movement and avoids stiffness.
optionExplanations.C: True. Stable fixation can promote union.
optionExplanations.D: True. Early mobilisation shortens hospital stay.
optionExplanations.E: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Rigid adult-type metal implants are not best suited to children with open physes.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the advantages and limits of internal fixation implants.

questions.question: This injury is:
questions.explanation: The radiograph shows a fracture running through the distal tibial physis and into the epiphysis and joint (arrow), consistent with Salter-Harris type III. It is an intra-articular physeal injury that needs anatomical reduction and risks growth arrest and arthritis.

optionExplanations.A: Not simple: physeal injuries carry risks of growth disturbance.
optionExplanations.B: This is not a fracture-dislocation pattern.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A fracture through the physis and epiphysis into the joint is Salter-Harris III.
optionExplanations.D: Salter-Harris II passes through the physis and exits via the metaphysis.
optionExplanations.E: The open physis shows this is a paediatric, not adult, injury.

questions.educationalObjective: Classify a physeal fracture as Salter-Harris III.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: Fracture non union maybe due to one / all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Non-union results from infection, excessive motion/instability, poor nutrition and devascularisation. Rigid, stable fixation promotes union and does not cause non-union.

optionExplanations.A: Infection is a recognised cause of non-union.
optionExplanations.B: Excessive motion at the fracture site prevents bridging callus.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Rigid fixation promotes union.
optionExplanations.D: Poor nutrition delays healing.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the causes of fracture non-union.

questions.question: 40 years old male complaining from knee pain, all are true differential diagnosis except:
questions.explanation: Differential diagnoses of knee pain in a 40-year-old include gout, septic arthritis (synovial WBC about 50,000) and a tibial fracture after trauma; a prior aseptic aspiration can introduce infection. Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of adolescents and is not a diagnosis in a 40-year-old.

optionExplanations.A: A true differential: uric acid crystals indicate gout.
optionExplanations.B: A true differential: synovial fluid WBC of about 50,000 suggests septic arthritis.
optionExplanations.C: A true differential: trauma suggests a tibial fracture.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Osgood-Schlatter affects adolescents with open tibial tubercle physis.
optionExplanations.E: A true differential: previous aspiration can introduce infection.

questions.educationalObjective: Build a differential diagnosis for knee pain in an adult.

questions.question: A 7 yr old girl with Hx of falling on outstretched hand , c/o severe Rt elbow pain , swelling and deformity What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A 7-year-old who falls on an outstretched hand and has severe elbow pain, swelling and deformity, with a radiograph showing a displaced distal humeral fracture, has a supracondylar fracture. The slide marks option B by yellow highlighting.

optionExplanations.A: Pulled elbow occurs in toddlers after traction and shows no swelling or deformity.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Supracondylar fracture is the typical elbow injury in this age group after a fall on the outstretched hand.
optionExplanations.C: Radial head fractures are more common in adults and cause lateral tenderness without gross deformity.
optionExplanations.D: The humeral head is at the shoulder, not the elbow.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose supracondylar humeral fracture in children.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: In this patient, One is Correct:

options.A: No shortening expected in the limb affected
options.D: This is a 19 year old patient

questions.explanation: The AP and lateral radiographs show a displaced femoral shaft fracture with open distal femoral physes. On the AP view the distal fragment lies medial to the proximal fragment (medial translation). The patient is a child (open growth plates), so the age of 19 is incorrect, and overlapping fragments imply shortening.

optionExplanations.A: A displaced, overriding fracture produces limb shortening.
optionExplanations.B: The statement about AP angulation toward the medial side is not supported by the film; the displacement seen is translation.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The distal fragment is translated medially on the AP view.
optionExplanations.D: Open distal femoral physes show a child, not a 19-year-old.

questions.educationalObjective: Describe displacement of fracture fragments on a radiograph (translation, angulation, shortening).

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: looking at the X rays, One statement from the below is Correct:

options.A: This is Salter Harris type I injury
options.B: Lateral view doesn’t meet the rule of TWO regarding joints that should appear
options.C: The X rays don’t meet the rule of TWO regarding views that should appear
options.D: We can see the two sides , so the rule of TWO regarding both sides is met here

questions.explanation: The 'rule of two' asks for two views, two joints (above and below), two sides when needed, and two occasions. Here both an AP and a lateral view are present, but the lateral view shows the hip and not the knee, so the two-joint rule is not met. Only one limb is shown, so both sides are not compared. The fracture is a shaft fracture, not a Salter-Harris I injury.

optionExplanations.A: The fracture runs through the femoral shaft, not the physis, so it is not Salter-Harris I.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The lateral view does not include both joints (the knee is missing).
optionExplanations.C: Both AP and lateral views are provided, so the views criterion is met.
optionExplanations.D: Only one side is imaged, so the two-sides rule is not met.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply the 'rule of two' in fracture imaging.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: If both dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries are intact, the Gustillo type of this fracture is:
questions.explanation: The photograph shows a large open wound with extensive soft-tissue loss and exposed bone that would need flap coverage. With intact dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses there is no arterial injury requiring repair, so this is Gustilo type IIIB (IIIC requires vascular injury needing repair).

optionExplanations.A: Type II has a wound of 1-10 cm without extensive soft-tissue damage.
optionExplanations.B: Type IIIA has adequate soft-tissue coverage of bone despite extensive laceration.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Extensive soft-tissue loss with exposed bone needing flap cover, with intact pulses, is type IIIB.
optionExplanations.D: Type IIIC needs an arterial injury requiring repair; pulses are intact here.

questions.educationalObjective: Classify open fractures using the Gustilo-Anderson system.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: The patient is conscious and this is the only injury, All of the following should be done in the Emergency Room EXCEPT:

options.B: Check if tetatnus immunization is needed

questions.explanation: In the emergency room the priorities for an open fracture are broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, copious irrigation and a sterile dressing with splinting. External fixation is performed in the operating theatre after formal debridement.

optionExplanations.A: Done early: IV antibiotics reduce infection risk.
optionExplanations.B: Done: check tetanus immunisation status.
optionExplanations.C: Done: copious saline irrigation removes gross contamination.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). External fixation is an operative step performed in theatre, not in the ER.

questions.educationalObjective: List emergency-room steps for an open fracture.

questions.question: Looking at her gait, this patient has :
questions.explanation: The photograph shows a woman walking while pressing a hand against the thigh to push the knee into extension, a sign of weak knee extensors (quadriceps) that cannot lock the knee at heel strike. Weak hip abductors give a Trendelenburg gait and weak extensors give a backward trunk lurch.

optionExplanations.A: Weak hip abductors cause a Trendelenburg gait with pelvic drop.
optionExplanations.B: Weak hip extensors cause a backward-leaning trunk lurch.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Hand pressed on the thigh to stabilise the knee indicates quadriceps (knee extensor) weakness.
optionExplanations.D: Weak knee flexors are not compensated by pressing on the thigh.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise a quadriceps-weakness gait.

questions.question: If her condition is due to nerve paralysis due to childhood infection, The microorganism is:
questions.explanation: Quadriceps weakness from nerve paralysis after childhood infection points to poliomyelitis, caused by the polio virus attacking anterior horn cells and leaving flaccid paralysis.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Poliovirus causes anterior horn cell loss and residual flaccid paralysis of limbs.
optionExplanations.B: Mumps virus causes parotitis, orchitis and meningitis, not limb paralysis.
optionExplanations.C: Diphtheria is caused by a bacterium (Corynebacterium diphtheriae), not a virus.
optionExplanations.D: Staphylococcus aureus causes osteomyelitis and septic arthritis, not nerve paralysis.

questions.educationalObjective: Link residual paralysis after childhood infection to poliomyelitis.

questions.question: This 72 yr old indian man has history of both knees progressive pain over years, Questions that are important to assess the severity of pain are the following EXCEPT

options.A: Are you able to do your daily activities without help?
options.B: Does the pain improve with pain killers & what are they?
options.C: Is it less or more severe than toothache?
options.D: Does this pain awaken you from sleep?

questions.explanation: Assessing pain severity in knee osteoarthritis relies on function (daily activities), response to analgesics and night pain. Comparing the pain with toothache is not a useful or standard question.

optionExplanations.A: Important: functional limitation reflects severity.
optionExplanations.B: Important: analgesic response and use show severity.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Comparison with toothache is not a standard assessment of knee pain severity.
optionExplanations.D: Important: night pain that wakes the patient indicates severe disease.

questions.educationalObjective: Take a focused pain history in knee osteoarthritis.

questions.question: This patient walks with:
questions.explanation: The photograph shows an elderly man with bowed legs, i.e. varus knees, from medial compartment osteoarthritis.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The bowed-leg appearance is genu varum.
optionExplanations.B: A Trendelenburg lurch is a trunk sway from abductor weakness.
optionExplanations.C: Valgus (knock-knee) is the opposite alignment.
optionExplanations.D: No walking aid is shown.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify varus deformity in knee osteoarthritis.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: This 35 yr old man jumped from a third floor on his heels, You expect all of the following conditions EXCEPT

options.B: Fluid or blood from ear, nose or throat

questions.explanation: A fall from height onto the heels transmits axial load: expect calcaneal fractures, compressed thoracolumbar vertebral fractures and skull base fractures (blood or fluid from ear, nose or throat). Rib fractures are not part of this pattern.

optionExplanations.A: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Rib fractures are not part of the axial-loading pattern.
optionExplanations.B: Expected: basal skull fracture may cause CSF/blood leakage from ear or nose.
optionExplanations.C: Expected: calcaneal fracture is the primary injury.
optionExplanations.D: Expected: axial load causes vertebral compression fractures.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the injury pattern after a fall onto the heels.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: The local complication that we expect in the first 24 hours is?
questions.explanation: Calcaneal fractures can cause compartment syndrome of the foot within the first 24 hours. Fat embolism is a systemic complication, DVT develops later, and malunion is a late local complication.

optionExplanations.A: Fat embolism is systemic and not a local complication.
optionExplanations.B: DVT is a systemic/vascular complication that develops later.
optionExplanations.C: Malunion becomes apparent weeks later.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Compartment syndrome develops in the first 24 hours after severe swelling.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise early local complications of calcaneal fractures.

questions.question: This 64 yr old woman who is severely complaining of both knees pain and stiffness insists that she want the operation to both knees at the same time, you have to tell her that risks of the following are more doing them together than doing them separately EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Simultaneous bilateral knee replacement carries higher risks of death, thromboembolism and bleeding than staged operations. It does not change the success of the local operation.

optionExplanations.A: Risk of death is higher with simultaneous surgery.
optionExplanations.B: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Local operative success is not increased.
optionExplanations.C: Thromboembolic risk is higher.
optionExplanations.D: Blood loss and transfusion needs are higher.

questions.educationalObjective: Counsel about simultaneous bilateral total knee replacement.

questions.question: This patient who doesn’t have any inflammatory or rheumatic disease, her X ray will show the following EXCEPT

options.B: Uneven narrowing of medial and lateral compartments
options.D: Deformity in the coronal plane of her knees

questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis shows osteophytes, uneven (asymmetric) joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis and coronal deformity (varus/valgus). Periarticular osteopenia is characteristic of inflammatory arthritis.

optionExplanations.A: Seen in OA.
optionExplanations.B: Seen in OA (asymmetric narrowing, usually medial compartment).
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Periarticular osteopenia suggests inflammatory arthritis, not OA.
optionExplanations.D: Seen in OA (varus or valgus deformity).

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise radiographic features of knee osteoarthritis.

questions.question: This 58yr old lady came to your orthopedic clinic c/o swelling in her both legs, most probably this is due to:

options.A: Orthopedic problem and treat her as ortho. case
options.D: Organ failure, refer to internal medicine

questions.explanation: Bilateral leg swelling in a 58-year-old is most likely systemic (cardiac, renal or hepatic failure, or similar), so referral to internal medicine is appropriate; it is not an orthopaedic problem or a normal finding.

optionExplanations.A: Bilateral oedema is unlikely to be a primary orthopaedic problem.
optionExplanations.B: Reassurance is inappropriate without excluding systemic disease.
optionExplanations.C: Lymphoedema (elephantiasis) is a less likely cause and would not be managed by vascular surgery by default.
optionExplanations.D: Correct per source. Systemic organ failure is the most probable cause and needs internal medicine referral.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise systemic causes of bilateral leg oedema.

questions.question: If she was your patient for the last five years for hip osteoarthritis and you treat her conservatively , You have to do all of the following related to your management EXCEPT:

options.A: High creatinine level could be related to your Rx
options.D: Check her activity level, maybe she doesn’t walk

questions.explanation: A patient treated conservatively for hip osteoarthritis for five years may have taken NSAIDs (renal impairment), may be inactive (ankle oedema), and her function should be reviewed. Expediting a total hip replacement is not an appropriate response to these systemic findings.

optionExplanations.A: Appropriate: NSAIDs may raise creatinine.
optionExplanations.B: Appropriate: take an NSAID history.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Expediting THR does not address the systemic problem.
optionExplanations.D: Appropriate: immobility may contribute to swelling.

questions.educationalObjective: Review systemic effects of long-term conservative treatment of hip osteoarthritis.

questions.question: Jordanian Patient: دكتور ايدي بتوجعني What is the best next question that you have to ask?

options.A: وين بالضبط ايدك بتوجعك؟ كتفك؟ ذراعك؟ كوعك؟ الساعد؟ الكف؟

questions.explanation: A patient says 'Doctor, my hand hurts'. The best next question is to localise the pain exactly (shoulder, arm, elbow, forearm, palm), since 'hand' may be used for any part of the upper limb. Onset, character and severity follow.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Localising the pain comes first because the complaint is vague.
optionExplanations.B: Onset duration is asked after localisation.
optionExplanations.C: Character of pain is explored after the site.
optionExplanations.D: Severity is assessed after the site and character.

questions.educationalObjective: Take a focused pain history, starting with site.

questions.question: The nurse after her doctor finished the history and before the examination: Doctor, I want to leave , my shift finished.

options.A: Tell the patient that he has to bring his own chaperon with him
options.B: Ask the nurse to stay with you till the end of the visit
options.C: Give her approval because this is the nurse’s right
options.D: The nurse should be a male nurse from the start as this is a male patient

questions.explanation: If the nurse acts as chaperone, she should stay for the whole examination. A chaperone must be present throughout the sensitive examination, and the patient should not be asked to bring one.

optionExplanations.A: The patient should not be asked to bring his own chaperone.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Ask the nurse to stay until the end of the visit.
optionExplanations.C: Leaving mid-visit leaves no chaperone for the examination.
optionExplanations.D: A male nurse is not required for a male patient.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply chaperone etiquette during examination.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: In the Ac, B, C, D and E survey , Ac stands for:
questions.explanation: In the ABCDE trauma survey, 'A' (Airway) includes cervical spine protection; 'Ac' stands for Airway with cervical spine control.

optionExplanations.A: Not the meaning of 'Ac'.
optionExplanations.B: Anticoagulant is not part of ABCDE.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Airway maintenance with cervical spine protection.
optionExplanations.D: Circulation is 'C'.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall the ABCDE trauma survey.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: wrapping a secured quilt or a belt around the pelvis to stabilize pelvic fracture is part of which step in the ABCDE survey
questions.explanation: A pelvic binder (secured quilt or belt around the pelvis) stabilises a pelvic fracture to control bleeding; it belongs to Circulation (haemorrhage control).

optionExplanations.A: Airway is not the step for pelvic stabilisation.
optionExplanations.B: Breathing is not the step for pelvic stabilisation.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Pelvic stabilisation controls haemorrhage in Circulation.
optionExplanations.D: Disability refers to neurological assessment.
optionExplanations.E: Exposure refers to full exposure and environmental control.

questions.educationalObjective: Place pelvic binder application in the ABCDE survey.

questions.question: This is caused by :
questions.explanation: The image shows a claw hand (hyperextended MCP and flexed IP joints of the ring and little fingers), typical of ulnar nerve injury. The slide's handwriting reads 'claw'.

optionExplanations.A: High radial nerve injury causes wrist drop.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Ulnar nerve injury causes claw hand.
optionExplanations.C: Dupuytren's contracture causes fixed flexion with palmar nodules, not sensory loss.
optionExplanations.D: Median nerve injury causes 'hand of benediction' or ape hand.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise claw hand as ulnar nerve injury.

questions.question: The sensation loss will be in:

options.E: Both Palmar and dorsal medial 1 ½ fingers

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies the palmar and dorsal surfaces of the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger; a lesion at the elbow or proximal wrist causes loss over both palmar and dorsal aspects of the medial 1.5 fingers.

optionExplanations.A: Palmar-only loss would occur if the dorsal branch were spared (lesion distal at the wrist).
optionExplanations.B: Palmar lateral 3.5 fingers is the median nerve distribution.
optionExplanations.C: Dorsal-only loss suggests the dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch only.
optionExplanations.D: Dorsal lateral 3.5 fingers is the radial/median dorsal distribution.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Both palmar and dorsal medial 1.5 fingers.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the cutaneous distribution of the ulnar nerve.

questions.question: The mechanism of this injury is:
questions.explanation: The radiograph shows a lateral tibial plateau fracture with depression. Lateral plateau fractures result from a valgus force (e.g. bumper injury) driving the lateral femoral condyle into the plateau.

optionExplanations.A: Distraction force produces avulsion injuries.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Valgus force causes lateral plateau fractures.
optionExplanations.C: Varus force produces medial plateau fractures.
optionExplanations.D: Torsional force produces spiral shaft fractures.

questions.educationalObjective: Relate tibial plateau fracture patterns to mechanism.

questions.question: This 22 year old runner who doesn’t remember any injury, felt mild pain in his midfoot for two weeks. He took NSAID’s , over the next three weeks he noticed an enlarging painless lump at the site of previous pain. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: A runner with insidious midfoot pain and a painless enlarging lump (callus) after weeks of rest/NSAIDs has a stress fracture with healing callus. The source answers the 3rd metatarsal.

optionExplanations.A: Osteosarcoma causes progressive pain, often at night, not a painless callus after rest.
optionExplanations.B: Chronic osteomyelitis would present with sinus, fever or systemic signs.
optionExplanations.C: The 4th metatarsal is less commonly affected.
optionExplanations.D: Correct per source. A 3rd metatarsal stress fracture with callus formation fits this history.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose a metatarsal stress fracture in a runner.

questions.question: Treatment for this injury is:

options.D: partial weight bearing on walker device

questions.explanation: The image is a hip radiograph showing an intertrochanteric fracture. The treatment is surgical fixation (ORIF, e.g. sliding hip screw or cephalomedullary nail) to allow early mobilisation.

optionExplanations.A: Casting is not suitable; it prevents early mobilisation and risks complications.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. ORIF is the standard treatment.
optionExplanations.C: Closed reduction and K-wires are not adequate fixation for this fracture.
optionExplanations.D: Partial weight bearing with a walker without fixation risks displacement and non-union.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage an intertrochanteric hip fracture surgically.

questions.question: This injury need :
questions.explanation: An intertrochanteric hip fracture should have ORIF within about 24-48 hours to reduce mortality and complications.

optionExplanations.A: Hip replacement is not the standard treatment for this fracture.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. ORIF within about 2 days is recommended.
optionExplanations.C: Reduction and casting is not used.
optionExplanations.D: Bed rest for a month raises morbidity and mortality.

questions.educationalObjective: State the timing of surgery for hip fractures.

questions.question: The name of this injury is:
questions.explanation: The fracture line runs between the greater and lesser trochanters (the lesser trochanter fragment is visible) - an intertrochanteric fracture.

optionExplanations.A: A neck of femur fracture is intracapsular and lies proximal to the trochanters.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The fracture lies between the trochanters.
optionExplanations.C: A subtrochanteric fracture lies below the lesser trochanter.

questions.educationalObjective: Name the type of proximal femoral fracture from the radiograph.

questions.question: One is TRUE about this injury :

options.B: closed reduction and casting within 48 hours
options.C: usually caused by high energy trauma

questions.explanation: Hip fractures in the elderly carry a one-year mortality of about 20-40%. They usually result from low-energy falls and are treated surgically; intertrochanteric fractures are fixed, not replaced.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Mortality is about 20-40%.
optionExplanations.B: Closed reduction and casting is not used.
optionExplanations.C: Usually low-energy trauma in osteoporotic elderly patients.
optionExplanations.D: Intertrochanteric fractures are fixed; replacement is used for displaced neck fractures.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall the mortality of hip fractures in the elderly.

questions.question: The head of the right femur is necrosed, the child has started to feel pain and limping for the last two months, One of the following is True about this patient:

options.A: The condition is called Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
options.B: this condition can be associated with coagulation disorders
options.C: This patient is twelve (12) year old

questions.explanation: The pelvic radiograph shows a dense, fragmented, flattened right femoral head with pain and limp for two months in a child: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease (idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head). It can be associated with coagulation disorders (thrombophilia). It typically affects ages 4-8, not SCFE adolescents.

optionExplanations.A: SCFE is a displacement of the proximal femoral epiphysis in adolescents; this is avascular necrosis (Perthes).
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Perthes disease can be associated with coagulation disorders.
optionExplanations.C: Perthes peaks at 4-8 years; 12 years is outside the typical range.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise Perthes disease and its associations.

questions.question: The head of the right femur is necrosed, the child has started to feel pain and limping for the last two months, One of the following is True about this patient:

options.A: The condition is called Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
options.B: may happen after Trauma or joint Effusion
options.C: This patient is twelve (12) year old

questions.explanation: The radiograph shows Perthes disease. Trauma or joint effusion (raising intracapsular pressure and compromising femoral head blood supply) has been proposed as a trigger.

optionExplanations.A: This is not SCFE.
optionExplanations.B: Correct per source. Trauma or effusion may precede the disease.
optionExplanations.C: A 12-year-old is older than the typical age range.

questions.educationalObjective: Know suspected triggers of Perthes disease.

questions.question: One of the following is True about this patient:

options.A: The condition is called Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
options.D: if his age was 5 years, he will have bad prognosis

questions.explanation: Perthes disease can occur with coagulation disorders. Management is often non-operative (containment, observation); surgery is used selectively. Younger onset (below 6 years) carries a better prognosis, so a 5-year-old would not do badly.

optionExplanations.A: This is Perthes disease, not SCFE.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Coagulation disorders can be associated.
optionExplanations.C: Not every patient needs surgery; many are managed conservatively.
optionExplanations.D: Younger children (about 5 years) have a better prognosis.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall prognostic factors in Perthes disease.

questions.question: The head of the right femur is necrosed, the child has started to feel pain and limping for the last two months, One of the following is True about this patient:

options.A: The condition is called Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
options.B: this condition can be associated with ADHD

questions.explanation: In a child with a necrotic right femoral head and limp for two months, Perthes disease is associated with ADHD. A 16-year-old would be too old for typical Perthes disease.

optionExplanations.A: Not SCFE.
optionExplanations.B: Correct per source. Perthes disease has a recognised association with ADHD.
optionExplanations.C: 16 years is too old for typical Perthes disease.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall associations of Perthes disease.

questions.question: 6 year old male, complain of right hip pain and limping, One is TRUE:

options.A: The condition is called Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
options.C: must be treated by femoral osteotomy

questions.explanation: A 6-year-old boy with hip pain and limp and a Perthes pattern on X-ray has a relatively good prognosis because of his young age (poorer when onset after about 8 years). Femoral osteotomy is only selectively used.

optionExplanations.A: This is not SCFE, which occurs in older, often overweight adolescents.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Onset around/under 6 years carries a good prognosis.
optionExplanations.C: Not all patients need femoral osteotomy.
optionExplanations.D: This is avascular necrosis, not neglected DDH.

questions.educationalObjective: Link age at onset to prognosis in Perthes disease.

questions.question: One of the following is true about diagnosis of this 1 year-old baby:

options.A: By physical examination left lower limb is longer than right using Galeazzi test
options.C: closed reduction, arthrogram, possible adductor tenotomy, and casting are treatment of choice

questions.explanation: The pelvic film of a 1-year-old shows a dislocated left hip (DDH). In a child aged about 6-18 months, treatment is closed reduction under anaesthesia with arthrogram, possible adductor tenotomy and spica casting. On Galeazzi testing the affected side appears shorter, not longer.

optionExplanations.A: In the Galeazzi test the dislocated side's knee is lower, i.e. the limb appears shorter.
optionExplanations.B: Open reduction is reserved for failed closed reduction or older children.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Closed reduction with arthrogram, possible adductor tenotomy and casting is the treatment of choice.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose treatment for DDH diagnosed around one year of age.

questions.question: One of the following is true about diagnosis of this baby:

options.A: By physical examination left lower limb is longer than right using Galeazzi test
options.B: such a disease may heal on its own ( without treatment)
options.C: After drawing Helgenreiner and Perkin’s lines and acetabular index, diagnosis is clear

questions.explanation: The pelvic film shows a dislocated left hip in a baby. Drawing Hilgenreiner's line, Perkin's line and measuring the acetabular index makes the diagnosis clear. A dislocated hip does not heal on its own and the dislocated limb appears shorter.

optionExplanations.A: On Galeazzi testing the dislocated limb appears shorter.
optionExplanations.B: An established dislocation does not resolve spontaneously.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. These lines and the acetabular index confirm DDH on the radiograph.

questions.educationalObjective: Use Hilgenreiner's and Perkin's lines and the acetabular index to diagnose DDH.

questions.question: One of the following is true about diagnosis of this baby:

options.A: By physical examination left lower limb is longer than right using Galeazzi test
options.C: will need open reduction and femoral shortening at 1 year of age
options.D: could be treated without surgery if detected at 4 months of age

questions.explanation: The pelvic film shows a left hip dislocation (DDH). The source marks open reduction with femoral shortening at 1 year of age as correct. However, DDH detected at 4 months can be treated without surgery (Pavlik harness), so option D is also true, and closed reduction is usually tried first at 1 year. [FLAG - More than one defensible answer: Option D is also a true statement (Pavlik harness at 4 months), and closed reduction is usually first-line at 1 year. The source key (C) was kept.]

optionExplanations.A: The dislocated limb appears shorter on Galeazzi testing.
optionExplanations.B: The left acetabulum is shallow/dysplastic, so it is not normal bilaterally.
optionExplanations.C: Marked as correct in the source.
optionExplanations.D: Also true in standard teaching: early detection at about 4 months is treated with a Pavlik harness without surgery.

questions.educationalObjective: Select management according to age at diagnosis of DDH.

questions.question: One of the following is true about this 1.5 year-old baby:

options.A: By physical examination left lower limb is longer than right using Galeazzi test
options.B: acetabular index angles are normal on both hips
options.C: during walking his body would lean towards the left side on stance phase

questions.explanation: In a 1.5-year-old with a left hip dislocation, the body leans toward the affected (left) side in stance (compensated Trendelenburg gait). The acetabular index is abnormal on the left, and the Galeazzi test shows the limb shorter.

optionExplanations.A: The affected limb appears shorter on Galeazzi testing.
optionExplanations.B: The acetabular index is increased on the dislocated side.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The trunk leans toward the affected side during stance phase.

questions.educationalObjective: Describe gait in unilateral DDH.

questions.question: If this was not a temporary intrauterine positional deformity, it is called:
questions.explanation: The photograph shows bilateral feet in equinus and varus with forefoot adduction: congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot), when not a temporary positional deformity.

optionExplanations.A: Tarsal coalition gives a rigid flat foot in older children.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Talipes equinovarus.
optionExplanations.C: Pes cavus is a high arch.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise congenital talipes equinovarus.

questions.question: One is FALSE about this condition:

options.A: serial manipulation and casting is gold standard of treatment
options.B: treatment starts at one month of age
options.D: correction of hindfoot varus must be done at last

questions.explanation: In idiopathic clubfoot, Ponseti serial manipulation and casting is the gold standard; deformity components are corrected in the order cavus, adductus, varus, then equinus last (often with an Achilles tenotomy). The statement that hindfoot varus is corrected last is therefore false. [FLAG - More than one defensible answer: Options B and C also contain inaccuracies (Ponseti casting starts in the first 1-2 weeks of life, and idiopathic clubfoot is a rigid deformity). The source key (D) was kept.]

optionExplanations.A: True: serial manipulation and casting is the gold standard.
optionExplanations.B: Stated as true in the source (treatment starts very early after birth).
optionExplanations.C: Stated as true in the source.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the FALSE option). Equinus, not hindfoot varus, is corrected last.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the Ponseti correction sequence for clubfoot.

questions.question: Treatment of this condition is:
questions.explanation: Congenital clubfoot is treated with serial manipulation and casting (Ponseti method), followed by bracing; tendon lengthening is only a late adjunct.

optionExplanations.A: Tendon lengthening is a limited step for residual equinus, not the primary treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Serial manipulation and casting.
optionExplanations.C: Home stretching alone is for positional deformities.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose first-line treatment of clubfoot.

questions.question: This condition is :
questions.explanation: The bilateral clubfoot is treated by manipulation and casting; stretching alone is not sufficient and surgery is not first-line at one month.

optionExplanations.A: Tarsal coalition is a rigid flatfoot in older children.
optionExplanations.B: Surgery at one month is not first-line.
optionExplanations.C: Stretching alone is insufficient for established clubfoot.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Manipulation and casting.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose first-line treatment of clubfoot.

questions.question: One is TRUE :

options.B: varus shoud be corrected after equinus correction

questions.explanation: [Answer determined independently: no answer was marked in the source.] No answer was marked on this slide. By Ponseti principles, correction proceeds as cavus, adductus, varus, then equinus last, so cavus is corrected first and varus is corrected before equinus. Tendon lengthening (Achilles tenotomy) is only a late step for residual equinus.

optionExplanations.A: Achilles tenotomy is only a late adjunct for residual equinus after casting; it is not the main treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Varus is corrected before equinus, not after it.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (independently determined). The cavus component is corrected first.

questions.educationalObjective: Order the corrections in Ponseti casting for clubfoot.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: If this man puts his right thumb at the maximum pain he experiences for the last few months, then he most probably has:
questions.explanation: A man placing his thumb at the point of maximal pain on the medial side of the elbow has medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow); lateral pain would be tennis elbow.

optionExplanations.A: Hitchhiker deformity is a diastrophic dysplasia feature, not elbow pain.
optionExplanations.B: Tennis elbow gives lateral epicondyle pain.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Golfer's elbow is medial epicondylitis.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate golfer's elbow from tennis elbow.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: The diagnosis of this X ray of a 55 year-old female patient is:
questions.explanation: The radiograph of a 55-year-old woman shows a calcific deposit (circled) near the humeral head: calcific tendonitis, not a dislocation or tuberosity fracture.

optionExplanations.A: The humeral head is located in the glenoid.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Calcific tendonitis.
optionExplanations.C: No fracture line is seen at the tuberosity.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose calcific tendonitis on a shoulder radiograph.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: The diagnosis of this X ray of a 55 year-old female patient is:
questions.explanation: The calcific deposit lies above the humeral head at the supraspinatus insertion, so calcific tendonitis of the supraspinatus.

optionExplanations.A: Subscapularis deposits lie anterior/medial.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Supraspinatus calcific tendonitis.
optionExplanations.C: No fracture is seen.

questions.educationalObjective: Localise calcific tendonitis to the rotator cuff tendon involved.

questions.question: The injury of this structure is:
questions.explanation: The arrow marks the medial side of the knee: a medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury, caused by a valgus force and tested by valgus stress; McMurray's test is for the meniscus.

optionExplanations.A: The arrow marks the medial side, not the lateral collateral ligament.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. MCL injury results from a valgus force.
optionExplanations.C: McMurray's test diagnoses meniscal injury.

questions.educationalObjective: Link MCL injury to valgus stress.

questions.question: Which special test is gold standard to diagnose the injured structure :

options.A: valgus stress test at 30 degree flexion
options.B: valgus stress test at 0 degree flexion

questions.explanation: Valgus stress at 30 degrees of flexion isolates the MCL; valgus stress at 0 degrees also loads the cruciate ligaments and posteromedial capsule. Apley's grind test assesses the menisci.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Valgus stress at 30 degrees of flexion.
optionExplanations.B: At 0 degrees the cruciates and posteromedial capsule also resist the stress.
optionExplanations.C: Apley's grind with distraction is a meniscal test.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose the test that best assesses the MCL.

questions.question: All of following are TRUE about injured structure EXCEPT :

options.A: diagnosed with valgus stress test at 30 degree flexion

questions.explanation: MCL injuries are diagnosed by valgus stress at 30 degrees of flexion and are often associated with meniscal (and ACL) injuries; they are not always associated with a PCL injury.

optionExplanations.A: True: valgus stress at 30 degrees.
optionExplanations.B: True: associated meniscal injury is common.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). It is not always associated with a PCL injury.

questions.educationalObjective: Know associated injuries of the MCL.

questions.question: One is correct :
questions.explanation: The arrow marks the medial knee: an MCL injury caused by valgus force and usually treated with a brace (non-operatively). It is not a lateral collateral ligament injury, varus injury or 90% associated with PCL injury.

optionExplanations.A: This is a medial, not lateral, ligament.
optionExplanations.B: MCL injury is caused by a valgus force.
optionExplanations.C: Not 90% associated with PCL injury.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. MCL injuries are usually treated with a brace.

questions.educationalObjective: Know non-operative treatment of MCL injuries.

questions.question: Regarding the deformity seen in the picture (the arrow points at deformity), One of the following is Correct :

options.C: Operative treatment is the best choice for acute first timer

questions.explanation: The photograph shows an acute patellar dislocation: the patella lies laterally with visible deformity. It results from a twisting non-contact injury and is treated by prompt reduction; first-time dislocations are managed non-operatively. The slide marks 'this is an emergency'.

optionExplanations.A: Correct per source. An acute dislocated patella needs prompt reduction.
optionExplanations.B: Usually a non-contact twisting injury.
optionExplanations.C: First-time dislocation is usually treated conservatively.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage acute patellar dislocation.

questions.question: This special test

options.A: is used to diagnose Anterior cruciate ligament injury
options.C: is used to diagnose PCL injury

questions.explanation: The knee is flexed 90 degrees and the tibia pulled forward: the anterior drawer test, used to diagnose ACL injury. Lachman's test is done at 20-30 degrees of flexion, and the posterior drawer test diagnoses PCL injury.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Anterior drawer test for ACL injury.
optionExplanations.B: Lachman is performed at about 20-30 degrees of flexion.
optionExplanations.C: PCL injury is diagnosed with the posterior drawer test.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise the anterior drawer test.

questions.question: This special test

options.A: is more sensitive than Lachman test
options.B: is more sensitive than Mcmurray test
options.C: is used to diagnose PCL injury
options.D: is used to diagnose ACL injury

questions.explanation: The shown test is the anterior drawer test for ACL injury; Lachman's test is more sensitive than the anterior drawer.

optionExplanations.A: Lachman's is more sensitive than the anterior drawer test.
optionExplanations.B: Meniscal tests such as McMurray assess a different structure.
optionExplanations.C: PCL injury is tested with the posterior drawer test.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Anterior drawer test for ACL injury.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the anterior drawer test and its sensitivity compared with Lachman.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: This patient has an injury in the left shoulder , The injury is abduction and external rotation with blow to the elbow, One of the following is correct:

options.C: No need for X ray if you reduce the joint

questions.explanation: Abduction and external rotation with a blow to the elbow produces anterior shoulder dislocation. Treatment is prompt (emergent) closed reduction, with radiographs before and after reduction and neurovascular assessment.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Emergent reduction is the treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Elective reduction delays treatment and increases pain and muscle spasm.
optionExplanations.C: Radiographs are needed before and after reduction.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage anterior shoulder dislocation.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: This patient has an injury in the left shoulder , The injury is abduction and external rotation with blow to the elbow, One of the following is correct:

options.A: Lesser tuberosity fracture can happen with this injury
options.B: Emergent surgical reduction should be done

questions.explanation: Anterior shoulder dislocation can injure the axillary nerve (check deltoid sensation/function). Greater (not lesser) tuberosity fractures accompany anterior dislocation; treatment is closed reduction; electric shock/seizure causes posterior dislocation.

optionExplanations.A: Greater tuberosity fractures accompany anterior dislocation; lesser tuberosity avulsion accompanies posterior dislocation.
optionExplanations.B: Closed reduction is the standard; surgical reduction is not usually required.
optionExplanations.C: Electric shock or seizures typically cause posterior dislocation.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Axillary nerve injury is a recognised complication.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall complications of anterior shoulder dislocation.

questions.question: The most correct statement of the following is :

options.A: In pic A, no osteophytes are seen in any of the two hips
options.B: In pic B, most probably it is inflammatory arthritis
options.C: No way that the patient in pic A has post traumatic arthritis

questions.explanation: Radiograph B shows symmetrical, uniform joint-space loss without osteophytes, in keeping with inflammatory arthritis, whereas radiograph A shows osteophyte formation compatible with osteoarthritis (possibly post-traumatic).

optionExplanations.A: Osteophytes are present in at least one hip in picture A.
optionExplanations.B: Correct per source. Picture B is most probably inflammatory arthritis.
optionExplanations.C: Post-traumatic arthritis cannot be excluded in picture A.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate inflammatory from degenerative hip arthritis radiographically.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: One of the following is correct regarding this problem:

options.A: Casting is the best treatment of choice
options.B: open reduction and repair must be done

questions.explanation: The picture shows a pulled elbow (radial head subluxation, nursemaid's elbow) in a toddler after a pull on the arm. It is treated by a simple reduction manoeuvre that is usually easily achieved; casting or open reduction are not needed.

optionExplanations.A: Casting is not the treatment; the problem is reduced by manoeuvre.
optionExplanations.B: Open reduction and repair are not required.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The reduction manoeuvre is usually easy and successful.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage pulled elbow with a reduction manoeuvre.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: One of the following is correct regarding this problem:

options.A: Casting is the best treatment of choice
options.B: open reduction and repair must be done
options.C: Reduction done by supinating wrist and flexing elbow
options.D: Reduction done by pronating the wrist and flexing the elbow

questions.explanation: Pulled elbow is reduced by supinating the forearm and flexing the elbow while pressing on the radial head (a hyperpronation technique is also accepted). [FLAG - More than one defensible answer: Option D (pronation with elbow flexion, the hyperpronation method) is also an accepted technique. The source key (C) was kept.]

optionExplanations.A: Casting is not the best treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Open reduction is not required.
optionExplanations.C: Correct per source. Supination of the wrist with elbow flexion reduces the subluxation.
optionExplanations.D: Pronation with flexion (the hyperpronation method) is also an accepted technique, so this statement is arguably also correct.

questions.educationalObjective: Describe the reduction technique for pulled elbow.

questions.question: The baby is irritable and doesn’t accept feeding in the Neonatal ICU, and have low fever, and refuse to move left lower limb Most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: A neonate that is irritable, refuses feeding, has a low fever and refuses to move the left lower limb has septic arthritis of the left hip until proven otherwise. DDH is painless and without fever; a femoral neck fracture needs significant trauma.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Pain, fever, refusal to feed and pseudoparalysis of the left limb indicate left hip septic arthritis.
optionExplanations.B: Femoral neck fracture in a neonate would need major trauma.
optionExplanations.C: DDH is painless and not associated with fever.
optionExplanations.D: The refusal to move the limb concerns the left side, not the right.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise neonatal septic arthritis of the hip.

questions.question: This 56 years old lady has been operated eight days ago, presented with severe pain, redness and fever. One of the following is correct:

options.B: order CRP, ESR and WBC’s, then aspirate the joint and send for culture and sensitivity
options.C: X-ray is the best investigation to diagnose the condition

questions.explanation: Eight days after surgery, severe pain, redness and fever of the operated knee suggest an infected knee wound/prosthesis (septic arthritis). Check inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, WBC) and aspirate the joint for culture and sensitivity before giving antibiotics.

optionExplanations.A: DVT presents with calf swelling and does not explain the red, hot surgical wound with fever.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Send CRP, ESR and WBC, then aspirate for culture and sensitivity.
optionExplanations.C: X-ray is not the best test for early infection.
optionExplanations.D: Starting oral antibiotics without cultures is inappropriate; infected prostheses need culture-directed IV therapy.

questions.educationalObjective: Investigate suspected post-operative joint infection.

questions.question: This 56 years old lady has been operated eight days ago, presented with severe pain, redness and fever. One of the following is correct:

options.B: Most common cause of this condition is caused by S. aureus
options.C: X-ray is the best investigation to diagnose the condition

questions.explanation: Postoperative joint and wound infection is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

optionExplanations.A: DVT does not explain the red, hot wound with fever.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. S. aureus is the most common causative organism.
optionExplanations.C: X-ray is not the best test for early infection.
optionExplanations.D: Oral antibiotics before cultures are inappropriate.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the commonest organism in postoperative orthopaedic infection.

questions.question: This X ray is for:

options.C: An adult patient with acute fracture

questions.explanation: The radiographs of the long bone show sclerosis, periosteal new bone and lucent areas with sequestrum-like densities: chronic osteomyelitis. Paget disease affects older adults, and an acute fracture would show a fracture line.

optionExplanations.A: Paget disease occurs in older adults with bone enlargement and coarse trabeculae.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Chronic osteomyelitis (sclerosis, periosteal reaction, sequestra).
optionExplanations.C: No acute fracture is demonstrated.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise radiographic features of chronic osteomyelitis.

questions.question: 33 year old male underwent surgical ORIF of his tibia, 3 months later he came to ER with the following image The management includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options.C: The current metal should be replaced by external fixator

questions.explanation: Three months after ORIF a draining wound over the tibia suggests deep infection. Management includes extensive debridement (often multiple sessions), replacing the current metal by an external fixator and IV antibiotics. Oral antibiotics at home alone are inadequate.

optionExplanations.A: Extensive debridement is part of management.
optionExplanations.B: Multiple debridement sessions may be needed.
optionExplanations.C: Infected hardware may be replaced by an external fixator.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Oral antibiotics alone at home are not adequate treatment.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan management of infection after fracture fixation.

questions.question: 33 year old male underwent surgical ORIF of his tibia, 6 months later he came to ER with the following image Most likely diagnosis is :
questions.explanation: Six months after ORIF, a draining sinus with chronic changes over the tibia indicates chronic osteomyelitis (implant-related). A venous ulcer occurs on the medial malleolus region with varicose changes, and an arterial ulcer occurs on the toes/pressure points.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Chronic osteomyelitis.
