optionExplanations.B: Venous ulcers have varicose skin changes and lie around the medial malleolus.
optionExplanations.C: Arterial ulcers occur at the toes or pressure points with absent pulses.
optionExplanations.D: Acute osteomyelitis develops over days to two weeks.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose chronic osteomyelitis after fracture fixation.

questions.question: This patient has:

options.B: A coronal plane deformity in the spine
options.D: This disease resolves spontaneously with time

questions.explanation: The back shows a lateral spinal curvature with trunk asymmetry: scoliosis, a deformity in the coronal plane. Scheuermann's disease is a sagittal-plane kyphosis; scoliosis does not resolve spontaneously and may progress.

optionExplanations.A: Scheuermann's disease is a thoracic kyphosis (sagittal plane).
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Scoliosis is a coronal-plane spinal deformity.
optionExplanations.C: An absent scapula is not the feature shown.
optionExplanations.D: Scoliosis may progress and does not resolve on its own.

questions.educationalObjective: Define scoliosis.

questions.question: This patient has:

options.D: This disease resolves spontaneously with time

questions.explanation: The photograph shows a lateral curvature of the spine with asymmetric shoulders and trunk, i.e. scoliosis.

optionExplanations.A: Scheuermann's disease is a kyphosis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Scoliosis.
optionExplanations.C: The scapula is present.
optionExplanations.D: Scoliosis does not resolve spontaneously.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise scoliosis from a clinical photograph.

questions.question: The most common cause of acute Low back pain (LBP) in this taxi driver is:
questions.explanation: The most common cause of acute low back pain in a taxi driver (prolonged sitting, vibration) is mechanical low back pain. Infection, cauda equina syndrome and disc prolapse are less common.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Mechanical low back pain.
optionExplanations.B: Infection is a rare cause.
optionExplanations.C: Cauda equina syndrome is a rare emergency.
optionExplanations.D: Disc prolapse is less common than mechanical back pain.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the commonest cause of acute low back pain.

questions.question: The most common cause of acute Low back pain (LBP) in this taxi driver is:
questions.explanation: The commonest cause of acute low back pain is musculoskeletal (mechanical) in origin.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Musculoskeletal.
optionExplanations.B: Infection is rare.
optionExplanations.C: Cauda equina syndrome is rare.
optionExplanations.D: Disc prolapse is less common.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the commonest cause of acute low back pain.

questions.question: 45 years old patient had this painful condition for one month, all of the following are TRUE except:

options.A: surgery is indicated if conservative treatment fails
options.B: could be treated by NSAID and splinting

questions.explanation: The image shows a trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis). It is treated with NSAIDs and splinting, cortisone injections and surgery (A1 pulley release) if conservative treatment fails; it is common in diabetics and in women older than 50, not in young males.

optionExplanations.A: True. Surgery is indicated if conservative treatment fails.
optionExplanations.B: True. NSAIDs and splinting may help.
optionExplanations.C: True. Cortisone injections help.
optionExplanations.D: True. It is common in diabetics.
optionExplanations.E: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). It is more common in middle-aged women, not young males.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall the epidemiology and treatment of trigger finger.

questions.question: 45 years old patient had this painful condition for one month, all of the following are TRUE except:
questions.explanation: Trigger finger is treated by A1 pulley release and cortisone injections and is common in diabetics and women older than 50. The Finkelstein test is used for De Quervain tenosynovitis, not trigger finger.

optionExplanations.A: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Finkelstein's test is for De Quervain tenosynovitis.
optionExplanations.B: True. A1 pulley release is the surgical treatment.
optionExplanations.C: True. Cortisone injections help.
optionExplanations.D: True. Common in diabetes.
optionExplanations.E: True. Common in females older than 50.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate trigger finger from De Quervain tenosynovitis.

questions.question: 45 years old Asian patient had this painful condition within short period of time, all of the following criteria are related except:
questions.explanation: The condition shown is related to trigger finger/flexor tendon stenosis, treated conservatively or with cortisone infiltration and correlated with rheumatoid arthritis. Autosomal dominant inheritance triggered by cirrhosis describes Dupuytren's disease, not this condition.

optionExplanations.A: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Autosomal dominant inheritance with cirrhosis relates to Dupuytren's disease.
optionExplanations.B: Related: conservative treatment is used.
optionExplanations.C: Related: cortisone infiltration helps.
optionExplanations.D: Related: associated with rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish risk associations of trigger finger from those of Dupuytren's disease.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: According to this Injury, If this patient completed the vaccination protocol and the last tetanus vaccine was 7-years ago, what should you give?
questions.explanation: An open tibial fracture is a tetanus-prone wound. If the patient completed the vaccination course and the last dose was 7 years ago (more than 5 years), a booster of the active vaccine alone is enough; immunoglobulin is for incomplete or unknown immunisation.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Booster of active tetanus vaccine only.
optionExplanations.B: Immunoglobulin alone is for those without immunisation.
optionExplanations.C: Both are given if immunisation is incomplete or unknown.
optionExplanations.D: A booster is needed because the last dose was more than 5 years ago.

questions.educationalObjective: Select tetanus prophylaxis in a fully immunised patient with a dirty wound.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: According to this Injury, one is TRUE:

options.C: Treated by debridement and external fixator

questions.explanation: The photograph and radiograph show an open fracture of the distal tibia and fibula with a wound at the fracture site. The source marks treatment by ORIF as correct. Standard teaching for a contaminated open fracture is debridement with external fixation (option C), so the key may be questioned. [FLAG - Uncertain / ambiguous: Debridement with external fixation (option C) is the standard approach for a contaminated open fracture, and the radiograph does not clearly show a pattern that suits primary ORIF. The source key (A) was kept.]

optionExplanations.A: Marked as correct in the source (ORIF).
optionExplanations.B: Dressing and casting is inadequate for an open fracture.
optionExplanations.C: Debridement and external fixator is the usual treatment for a contaminated open tibial fracture.
optionExplanations.D: Amputation is only for unsalvageable limbs.

questions.educationalObjective: Select treatment for an open distal tibial fracture.

questions.question: 33 years old patient complaining of this swelling, best statement about this lesion is

options.A: Origin of it, is from the substance of the joint capsule or the fibrous tendon sheath
options.C: The cause of this lesion is the plastic bracelet of his watch

questions.explanation: A well-defined swelling on the dorsum of the wrist is a ganglion cyst, which arises from the joint capsule or tendon sheath. Aspiration is not the best treatment (high recurrence); the watch is not the cause; ganglia are often symptomatic.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Ganglia arise from the joint capsule or tendon sheath.
optionExplanations.B: Aspiration has a high recurrence rate.
optionExplanations.C: The plastic bracelet is not the cause.
optionExplanations.D: Ganglia are not always asymptomatic.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the origin of a wrist ganglion.

questions.question: 33 years old patient complaining of this swelling, true statement about this lesion is

options.A: It may arising from scapho-lunate ligament
options.C: The cause of this lesion is the plastic bracelet of his watch

questions.explanation: A dorsal wrist ganglion usually arises from the scapholunate ligament/joint.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. It may arise from the scapholunate ligament.
optionExplanations.B: Aspiration has a high recurrence rate.
optionExplanations.C: The plastic bracelet is not the cause.
optionExplanations.D: Ganglia are not always asymptomatic.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the usual origin of a dorsal wrist ganglion.

questions.question: 69 years old female, with fever, if the blood WBC, CRP and ESR are high, the very next step in management is:

options.D: Sterile dressing with local antibiotic cream

questions.explanation: A 69-year-old with fever, a red swollen ankle and raised WBC, CRP and ESR may have septic arthritis. The next step is joint aspiration for cell count, Gram stain and culture, before antibiotics.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Joint aspiration comes first for diagnosis and cultures.
optionExplanations.B: Surgical debridement follows a confirmed diagnosis.
optionExplanations.C: IV antibiotics are given after cultures are taken.
optionExplanations.D: Dressing and cream are not adequate.

questions.educationalObjective: Take the first step in suspected septic arthritis.

questions.question: All these movements could predispose to a clinical condition One of the following is true about this condition:

options.A: Finklestein test is positive in this condition
options.B: Phallen test is positive in this condition
options.C: Incision and drainage is the treatment
options.D: The muscles affected are opponent pollicis and abductor pollices brevis

questions.explanation: Repetitive thumb movements (knitting, texting, gaming) predispose to De Quervain tenosynovitis, which has a positive Finkelstein test. The affected tendons are abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis. Phalen's test is for carpal tunnel syndrome.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Finkelstein's test is positive in De Quervain tenosynovitis.
optionExplanations.B: Phalen's test is for carpal tunnel syndrome.
optionExplanations.C: Incision and drainage is not the treatment.
optionExplanations.D: The affected muscles are abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise De Quervain tenosynovitis and its diagnostic test.

questions.question: All these movements could predispose to a clinical condition One of the following is true about this condition:

options.A: Hawkin’s test is positive in this condition
options.B: Phalen test is positive in this condition
options.C: Cortisone injection is first line of treatment
options.D: The tendons affected are extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus

questions.explanation: De Quervain tenosynovitis involves the first dorsal compartment tendons, extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus. Hawkins test is for shoulder impingement and Phalen's test for carpal tunnel syndrome.

optionExplanations.A: Hawkins' test is a shoulder test.
optionExplanations.B: Phalen's test is for carpal tunnel syndrome.
optionExplanations.C: Conservative measures (splint, NSAIDs) are usually tried before cortisone injection, which the source treats as incorrect here.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. EPB and APL tendons are affected.

questions.educationalObjective: Name the tendons involved in De Quervain tenosynovitis.

questions.question: This 50 years old female cannot extend her Thumb at Interphalngeal joint, all are true statements EXCEPT :

options.A: Tender thickening is felt opposite to metacarpal head
options.B: Steroid injection could cure the case
options.C: Role of surgery is there in this condition
options.D: Age group affected of such condition is adult group only

questions.explanation: The inability to extend the thumb IP joint with a tender nodule opposite the metacarpal head is trigger thumb. Tender thickening at the A1 pulley, steroid injection and surgery are all valid; the condition may also be congenital, so it is not limited to adults.

optionExplanations.A: True. Tender thickening is felt over the A1 pulley opposite the metacarpal head.
optionExplanations.B: True. Steroid injection can cure the condition.
optionExplanations.C: True. Surgery has a role.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Trigger thumb also occurs in children (congenital).

questions.educationalObjective: Recall features of trigger thumb.

questions.question: This 50 years old female cannot extend her Thumb at Interphalngeal joint, all are true statements EXCEPT :

options.A: Tenderness is felt over A2 pulley
options.B: Steroid injection could cure the case
options.C: Role of surgery is there in this condition

questions.explanation: In trigger thumb, tenderness is over the A1 pulley at the metacarpophalangeal level, not the A2 pulley. Steroid injection can cure it, surgery is an option and congenital forms exist.

optionExplanations.A: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). The tender nodule lies over the A1 pulley, not A2.
optionExplanations.B: True. Steroid injection can cure the condition.
optionExplanations.C: True. Surgery has a role.
optionExplanations.D: True. The condition can be congenital.

questions.educationalObjective: Localise the pathology in trigger digits to the A1 pulley.

questions.question: 15 years old patient complaining from anterior knee pain especially after running, no Hx of trauma, normal blood tests, normal Range Of Motion. One of the following is True

options.A: Surgical correction is the mainstay treatment
options.D: It is an Apophysitis of tibial tuberosity

questions.explanation: A 15-year-old with anterior knee pain after running, no trauma, normal blood tests and a prominence at the tibial tuberosity (yellow arrow) has Osgood-Schlatter disease: apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity. It is managed conservatively.

optionExplanations.A: Surgery is rarely needed.
optionExplanations.B: Antibiotics are not indicated; blood tests are normal.
optionExplanations.C: Ice, not hot water, is used after activity.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. It is an apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose Osgood-Schlatter disease.

questions.question: 15 years old patient complaining from anterior knee pain especially after running, no Hx of trauma, normal blood tests, normal Range Of Motion. One of the following is True

options.C: Aspiration is first line of treatment
options.D: Pain will go away after age of 17 years

questions.explanation: Osgood-Schlatter disease is self-limiting and the pain resolves once the apophysis closes, around age 17.

optionExplanations.A: Casting is not the mainstay treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Antibiotics are not indicated.
optionExplanations.C: Aspiration is not a treatment.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Pain settles as the apophysis fuses, about age 17.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the natural history of Osgood-Schlatter disease.

questions.question: This injury called
questions.explanation: The radiograph shows a fracture passing through the epiphysis, physis and metaphysis (blue arrows), i.e. Salter-Harris type IV, as marked on the slide.

optionExplanations.A: Type II passes through the physis and metaphysis only.
optionExplanations.B: Type III passes through the physis and epiphysis only.
optionExplanations.C: Correct per source. Salter-Harris IV involves epiphysis, physis and metaphysis.
optionExplanations.D: Type I is a fracture through the physis only.

questions.educationalObjective: Classify a Salter-Harris IV injury.

questions.question: One is TRUE about this injury in 12 year-old boy :
questions.explanation: A Salter-Harris IV injury crosses the physis and joint, so it is treated with anatomic reduction and fixation with lag screws to prevent growth arrest and articular incongruity.

optionExplanations.A: Salter-Harris II does not cross the epiphysis.
optionExplanations.B: Salter-Harris III does not cross the metaphysis.
optionExplanations.C: Closed reduction and casting is inadequate for an intra-articular physeal fracture.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Anatomic reduction and lag screw fixation.

questions.educationalObjective: Treat Salter-Harris IV fractures.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: According to this injury, One of the following is CORRECT:

options.A: Median nerve (anterior interosseus) is the most commonly affected
options.B: Only Immobilisation without reduction is sufficient
options.C: This injury is not common in children
options.D: Reduction must be done immediately in the ER even if no ischemic signs

questions.explanation: The lateral radiograph shows a displaced supracondylar humeral fracture. The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve is the most commonly affected nerve. The injury is common in children, needs reduction and fixation, and is an emergency only with a pulseless or ischaemic limb.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The anterior interosseous nerve is the most commonly injured nerve.
optionExplanations.B: Displaced fractures need reduction, not immobilisation alone.
optionExplanations.C: It is a common paediatric fracture.
optionExplanations.D: Emergency reduction in the ER is needed with ischaemic signs, not if there are none.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the commonest nerve injury in supracondylar fractures.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: According to this injury, One of the following is CORRECT:

options.A: Ulnar nerve is the most commonly affected nerve
options.B: Closed reduction and casting is sufficient
options.C: This injury is not common in children
options.D: Reduction must be done immediately in the ER if there is pulseless limb

questions.explanation: A displaced supracondylar fracture with a pulseless limb needs immediate reduction to restore circulation. The anterior interosseous nerve, not the ulnar nerve, is most commonly injured; closed reduction and casting alone is not sufficient for displaced fractures.

optionExplanations.A: The anterior interosseous (median) nerve is more commonly injured.
optionExplanations.B: Displaced fractures need reduction with pinning.
optionExplanations.C: It is a common paediatric fracture.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A pulseless limb needs immediate reduction in the ER.

optionExplanations.C: The navicular is dislocated dorsally on the talus.

questions.question: This is 40 years old lady, with right knee pain, decreased ROM for 5 days, history of twisting trauma on slippery floor before 1 week, one of the following is MOST LIKELY diagnosis:

optionExplanations.B: Cultures and IV antibiotics without removal are inadequate.

optionExplanations.B: Weakness of both lower limbs is expected with a lumbar-level compression.
optionExplanations.C: Marked as correct in the source (tachycardia).
optionExplanations.D: Bradycardia occurs in neurogenic shock after high cord injury, not lumbar compression.
optionExplanations.E: Exaggerated reflexes indicate upper motor neuron lesions; cauda equina compression causes reduced reflexes.

questions.educationalObjective: Predict signs after lumbar spinal compression.

questions.question: In this patient, you expect all of the following symptoms to be positive in the history of present illness EXCEPT?

options.A: Dashboard injury in a high speed car
options.B: The history is taken from an eye witness

questions.explanation: A high-speed dashboard injury with deformity and inability to walk suggests posterior hip dislocation. The patient cannot bear weight, so abnormal gait (limping) is not expected; history may come from an eyewitness.

optionExplanations.A: Expected: the mechanism is a dashboard injury in a high-speed car.
optionExplanations.B: Expected: the history may come from an eyewitness.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). The patient cannot walk, so limping is not expected.
optionExplanations.D: Expected: visible deformity.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise the history of a posterior hip dislocation.

questions.question: This 15/15 GCS normally communicating 23 yr old patient developed drop foot after MVA, Before you see this X ray, your top priority DDX of the lower limb injury include all of the following EXCEPT?
questions.explanation: After a motor vehicle accident, a drop foot suggests a lower limb injury: pelvic or proximal femur fracture, soft-tissue injury or hip dislocation (sciatic nerve injury). A cerebrovascular accident is not a top priority in a fully conscious, normally communicating 23-year-old.

optionExplanations.A: A priority diagnosis after high-energy trauma.
optionExplanations.B: A priority diagnosis.
optionExplanations.C: A priority diagnosis (sciatic nerve injury after posterior dislocation).
optionExplanations.D: All three are valid.
optionExplanations.E: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). CVA is unlikely in a young, fully conscious trauma patient.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritise differentials for drop foot after high-energy trauma.

questions.question: In this patient, ALL of the following are true EXCEPT?

options.A: Dashboard injury in a high speed car

questions.explanation: The radiograph shows a posterior hip dislocation after a dashboard injury, which can cause drop foot from sciatic nerve injury. An anterior dislocation is not present.

optionExplanations.A: True: dashboard injury is the mechanism.
optionExplanations.B: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). The dislocation is posterior, not anterior.
optionExplanations.C: True: posterior hip dislocation.
optionExplanations.D: True: sciatic nerve injury can cause drop foot.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the posterior hip dislocation on radiograph.

questions.question: This 15/15 GCS normally communicating, hemodynamically stable 23 yr old patient developed this isolated injury in the xray after MVA, your initial management of the lower limb injury include one of the following?
questions.explanation: A haemodynamically stable patient with an isolated hip dislocation needs emergent closed reduction (to reduce the risk of avascular necrosis and nerve damage).

optionExplanations.A: Elective reduction delays treatment.
optionExplanations.B: The patient is stable; transfusion is not indicated.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Emergent closed hip reduction.
optionExplanations.D: Open reduction is only for failed closed reduction.
optionExplanations.E: Skin traction does not reduce a dislocation.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage a hip dislocation.

questions.question: If your patient is a doctor, and he told you I think I have a tumor in my Rt arm discovered yesterday, you write the chief complaint in your history as:

options.A: Tumor in the Rt arm of one day duration
options.B: Elaborate تحقق أكثر more before writing the chief complaint
options.C: He just wants to show you his muscles, so just ignore writing his chief complaint
options.D: If he said tumor then write it as mass or swelling of Rt arm of one day duration

questions.explanation: In history taking, the chief complaint should record the patient's own words after clarifying them. A doctor who says he has a tumour should be asked to elaborate (what exactly he noticed) before the chief complaint is written. The source key is B.

optionExplanations.A: Writing 'tumour' records the patient's interpretation without clarification.
optionExplanations.B: Correct per source. Elaborate more before writing the chief complaint.
optionExplanations.C: Ignoring the complaint is unprofessional.
optionExplanations.D: Rewriting 'tumour' as 'mass or swelling' replaces the patient's words with the examiner's interpretation before clarifying what he actually noticed.

questions.educationalObjective: Write a chief complaint when a patient offers a self-diagnosis.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: If this patient was diagnosed with spiral humerus fracture after gunshot injury,best management will be :
questions.explanation: Gunshot injury with a spiral humeral fracture (and nerve-injury concern) is managed with external fixation and observation, avoiding extensive internal hardware in a contaminated wound.

optionExplanations.A: Casting alone does not stabilise the fracture adequately.
optionExplanations.B: ORIF with plate and nerve exploration is not recommended in a contaminated wound.
optionExplanations.C: IM nailing is not preferred for a gunshot wound.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. External fixation and observation.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage a humeral fracture after a gunshot injury.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: If the same patient is surgically (abdomen and chest) and neuro-surgically free but he lost 1.5 Lit. blood inside his pelvis , the measures to control his shock include all EXCEPT

options.A: Two IV lines and draw blood for Hb, X matching and ABO grouping
options.C: Urgent operation for internal fixation to control bleeding
options.D: Give 6 units of plasma and 6 units of platelets after each 6 units of blood

questions.explanation: In pelvic haemorrhage with shock, resuscitation includes two IV lines with blood draw and cross-matching, IV fluids, and balanced transfusion (plasma and platelets). Urgent internal fixation is not the immediate way to control bleeding (use a pelvic binder, external fixation, angio-embolisation or packing).

optionExplanations.A: Appropriate: two large-bore IV lines and blood tests.
optionExplanations.B: Appropriate: IV fluids.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Urgent internal fixation is not a first measure to control pelvic bleeding.
optionExplanations.D: Appropriate: balanced massive transfusion.

questions.educationalObjective: Control haemorrhagic shock from a pelvic fracture.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: This patient patient in the picture was brought to you by ambulance unconscious, the next step is:

options.C: Clean the blood from his face
options.D: Initiate ATLS protocol in the ER

questions.explanation: An unconscious trauma patient arriving by ambulance needs the ATLS primary survey (airway with cervical spine protection, breathing, circulation) before a full history or cosmetic cleaning.

optionExplanations.A: A full history comes after stabilisation.
optionExplanations.B: Intubation is decided within the airway assessment, not automatically.
optionExplanations.C: Cleaning the face is not a priority.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Initiate ATLS.

questions.educationalObjective: Start with ATLS in an unconscious trauma patient.

questions.question: If the patient in the picture has only that finger your differential diagnosis include all of the following EXCEPT

options.B: Avulsion fracture of distal phalanx with extensor tendon attached
options.C: Burn at the skin of palmar aspect of DIP crease
options.D: Deep Flexor tendon of the middle finger is cut
options.E: If this is reversible, then the patient can do it intentionally

questions.explanation: A finger held in flexion at the DIP joint can be a mallet finger, an avulsion fracture of the distal phalanx with the extensor tendon attached, a burn contracture at the palmar DIP crease, or voluntary. A cut deep flexor tendon would cause loss of DIP flexion, not a flexion deformity.

optionExplanations.A: A valid diagnosis: mallet finger.
optionExplanations.B: A valid diagnosis: bony mallet.
optionExplanations.C: A valid cause: burn contracture.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). A cut flexor tendon leaves the DIP unable to flex.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate causes of a flexed DIP joint.

questions.question: If this deformity is multiple and with other deformities in both hands, you expect:

options.A: Symmetrical bilateral arthritis in large joints
options.D: Osteophytes at sides of hips and knees

questions.explanation: Multiple finger deformities in both hands suggest rheumatoid arthritis, which causes symmetrical bilateral arthritis. Gout is not associated with such symmetry; osteophytes at hips and knees describe osteoarthritis; ulnar deviation occurs at the MCP joints, not at the wrist (the wrist deviates radially). [FLAG - Uncertain / ambiguous: Rheumatoid arthritis characteristically involves small joints (symmetrical polyarthritis), so 'large joints' is imprecise. The source key (A) was kept.]

optionExplanations.A: Correct per source. Rheumatoid arthritis causes symmetrical polyarthritis.
optionExplanations.B: High uric acid suggests gout.
optionExplanations.C: Ulnar deviation occurs at the MCP joints; the wrist deviates radially.
optionExplanations.D: Osteophytes at hips and knees indicate osteoarthritis.

questions.educationalObjective: Link multiple symmetrical hand deformities to rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.question: If the patient in the picture had no associated fractures, best management is:
questions.explanation: A mallet finger without an associated fracture is treated with continuous extension splinting of the DIP joint for about six to eight weeks.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Extension splinting.
optionExplanations.B: Tendon repair is not usually required.
optionExplanations.C: Physiotherapy alone does not hold the tendon ends together.
optionExplanations.D: Closed reduction and casting is used for fractures.

questions.educationalObjective: Treat mallet finger with splinting.

questions.question: If this deformity happened after the finger was jammed by car door , you expect :
questions.explanation: A finger jammed in a car door can avulse the extensor tendon from the distal phalanx, causing mallet finger (extensor tendon injury).

optionExplanations.A: A flexor tendon injury would cause loss of flexion.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Extensor tendon injury.
optionExplanations.C: Joint dislocation would show a different deformity.
optionExplanations.D: Collateral ligament injury causes lateral instability.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the mechanism and injury in mallet finger.

questions.question: Blood tests are useful in orthopedics in all of the following EXCEPT

options.B: Diagnose Calcium metabolic diseases like rickets
options.C: Bence Jones protein for multiple myeloma
options.D: Acute phase reactants like ESR and CRP are high in infections and cancers

questions.explanation: Blood tests are useful pre-operatively, for metabolic bone disease such as rickets, and acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP) are raised in infection and cancer. Bence Jones protein is detected in urine, not blood.

optionExplanations.A: Useful: pre-operative assessment.
optionExplanations.B: Useful: calcium, phosphate and vitamin D screen for rickets.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Bence Jones protein is found in urine.
optionExplanations.D: Useful: ESR and CRP are acute-phase reactants.

questions.educationalObjective: Know that Bence Jones proteins are a urine test.

questions.question: This DEXA scan:

options.B: This is radionuclide scan for tumors and infection
options.C: Screen all people of all ages
options.D: A treatment for low back pain

questions.explanation: The image shows a full-body DEXA bone densitometry scan with T-score graph, used to diagnose osteoporosis. It is not a radionuclide scan, not a screening for everyone and not a back pain treatment.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. DEXA diagnoses osteoporosis.
optionExplanations.B: A radionuclide (bone) scan is a different test.
optionExplanations.C: DEXA is not done on all people of all ages.
optionExplanations.D: DEXA is a diagnostic test, not a treatment.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise a DEXA scan and its use.

questions.question: Osteoporotic patients have increased fracture risk of all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Osteoporotic fractures typically occur in the spine, hip and distal radius (and proximal humerus). Metatarsal fractures are not typical osteoporotic fractures.

optionExplanations.A: Increased risk: vertebral fractures.
optionExplanations.B: Increased risk: hip fractures.
optionExplanations.C: Increased risk: distal radius fractures.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the EXCEPT answer). Metatarsal fractures are not classic osteoporotic fractures.

questions.educationalObjective: List typical osteoporotic fracture sites.

questions.question: This DEXA scan:

options.A: Is used to screen bone density after low energy hip fractures
options.B: Is used to measure calcium in hip and spine
options.D: Detect humerus fracture risk in elderly

questions.explanation: DEXA is used to measure bone mineral density, for example to screen for osteoporosis after a low-energy hip fracture. It does not measure calcium directly, is not limited to elderly women and does not detect humerus fracture risk specifically.

optionExplanations.A: Correct per source. Used to assess bone density after low-energy hip fractures.
optionExplanations.B: It measures bone mineral density, not serum calcium.
optionExplanations.C: It is not restricted to elderly females.
optionExplanations.D: It does not specifically detect humerus fracture risk.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the indication for DEXA scanning.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: The correct type of such injury post op is?
questions.explanation: The leg with an external fixator and a large soft-tissue wound requiring coverage is a Gustilo-Anderson type IIIB open fracture.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Type IIIB.
optionExplanations.B: Type II has a moderate wound without extensive soft-tissue stripping.
optionExplanations.C: Type IIIC includes an arterial injury requiring repair.
optionExplanations.D: Type IIIA has adequate soft-tissue cover of the bone.

questions.educationalObjective: Classify an open fracture by Gustilo-Anderson.

questions.question: The 4 tests shown here are used to diagnose:
questions.explanation: The four tests shown (joint line palpation, McMurray, Apley and Thessaly-type tests) assess for meniscal tears.

optionExplanations.A: ACL tests are the Lachman and drawer tests.
optionExplanations.B: Osteoarthritis is not diagnosed by these tests.
optionExplanations.C: MCL injury is tested with valgus stress.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Meniscus tear.

questions.educationalObjective: Name tests for meniscal injury.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Shoulder, Elbow and Upper Limb
questions.question: In this injury you have to examine least likely:
questions.explanation: The radiograph appears to show a displaced elbow (supracondylar humeral) fracture; the source does not name the injury. The neurovascular exam includes radial pulse and capillary refill and the OK sign (anterior interosseous nerve, the most commonly injured nerve). The hitchhiker (thumb extension) test for the radial nerve is the least likely of these to be examined according to the source.

optionExplanations.A: Important: assess vascular status.
optionExplanations.B: Important: the OK sign tests the anterior interosseous nerve.
optionExplanations.C: Correct per source. It is the least likely test to be examined.
optionExplanations.D: Important: capillary refill assesses perfusion.

questions.educationalObjective: Assess the neurovascular status after an elbow fracture.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: 20 year male presented to ER with closed MIDSHAFT tibia/fibula fracture due to MVA, after 1 hour of admission and splinting , he started to have severe pain, most likely diagnosis:
questions.explanation: A tibial shaft fracture with severe, increasing pain after splinting should make one think of acute compartment syndrome, not DVT, nerve injury or insufficient analgesia.

optionExplanations.A: DVT does not present with severe early pain.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Compartment syndrome.
optionExplanations.C: Nerve injury does not explain increasing severe pain after splinting.
optionExplanations.D: Insufficient analgesia is the diagnosis of exclusion.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose compartment syndrome after a tibial fracture.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Fractures, Trauma and Emergency Care
questions.question: Best management for his condition :
questions.explanation: The first step is to remove the splint and constrictive dressings and re-evaluate; if compartment syndrome persists, urgent fasciotomy follows.

optionExplanations.A: Fasciotomy follows if symptoms persist after removing the splint.
optionExplanations.B: Correct per source. Remove the splint and re-evaluate.
optionExplanations.C: Narcotics only mask the symptoms.
optionExplanations.D: External fixation does not treat compartment syndrome.

questions.educationalObjective: Take the first step in suspected compartment syndrome.

questions.question: This special test used to diagnose:
questions.explanation: The drawing shows a supine patient contracting the quadriceps with the knee flexed: the quadriceps active test, which diagnoses PCL injury (tibial sag reduces with quadriceps contraction).

optionExplanations.A: ACL injury is tested with Lachman or anterior drawer.
optionExplanations.B: Collateral ligaments are tested with varus/valgus stress.
optionExplanations.C: Patellar instability uses the apprehension test.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Quadriceps active test for PCL injury.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise the quadriceps active test for PCL injury.

questions.question: All of the following may cause knee locking EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Locked knee results from a displaced meniscal tear, a loose body or an ACL stump or tear that blocks extension. Patellar dislocation is the exception according to the source. [FLAG - Uncertain / ambiguous: An acutely dislocated patella can also leave the knee 'stuck' in flexion; the item is ambiguous. The source key (D) was kept.]

optionExplanations.A: A cause: displaced meniscal tear.
optionExplanations.B: A cause: loose body.
optionExplanations.C: A cause: ACL tear (displaced stump).
optionExplanations.D: Correct per source (the EXCEPT answer). Patellar dislocation.

questions.educationalObjective: List causes of knee locking.

questions.question: This test shown here are used to diagnose:
questions.explanation: The photographs show the McMurray (rotation with flexion/extension) test performed to detect meniscal tears; as marked in the source, the medial meniscus.

optionExplanations.A: ACL injuries are tested with Lachman or drawer tests.
optionExplanations.B: MCL injury is tested with valgus stress.
optionExplanations.C: A lateral meniscus tear is tested with the opposite rotation.
optionExplanations.D: Correct per source. Medial meniscus tear.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognise the McMurray test.

questions.question: 10 year old child complaining of left proximal arm pain with swelling of 6 weeks duration, WBC 19000, CRP 55 The best treatment is:
questions.explanation: A 10-year-old with six weeks of proximal arm pain, swelling, raised WBC and CRP, and a radiograph showing a lytic lesion with periosteal reaction, has subacute osteomyelitis with an abscess or sequestrum that needs surgical drainage and debridement.

optionExplanations.A: Oral antibiotics alone cannot treat an established abscess.
optionExplanations.B: IV antibiotics alone are insufficient when there is a collection.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Surgical debridement.
optionExplanations.D: External fixation is not needed.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage subacute osteomyelitis with abscess formation.

questions.question: one is TRUE:

options.D: Closed reduction and casting is the best treatment

questions.explanation: A forearm fracture in a child with open physes is usually treated by closed reduction and casting, because remodelling tolerates imperfect reduction. Anatomic reduction and surgery are not necessary, and a 30-year-old would have closed physes.

optionExplanations.A: The physes are open, so the patient is a child, not 30 years old.
optionExplanations.B: Anatomical reduction is not necessary in children due to remodelling.
optionExplanations.C: Surgery is not always required.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Closed reduction and casting is the best treatment.

questions.educationalObjective: Treat paediatric forearm fractures with closed reduction and casting.
